paragraphs.core_text: At the time when the F[ir]st [Man ...] he gave the leadership to his five [sons ... the] Living Spirit and the Mother of Life [...] as the entire ruling-power is entwined and crucified [...] they were poured out and mixed with each other, the light with the Darkness and the Darkness with the light.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue frame formula: '[Once again] the enlightener [speaks]:'
paragraphs.temporal_note: Frame formula wraps substrate cosmological teaching about the primordial event: First Man's sacrifice of five sons, the resulting mixture of light and darkness. High substrate score (21.67). The teaching describes the foundational cosmological event — the mixing — in impersonal process language. 'Entwined and crucified' and 'poured out and mixed' are systematic cosmic process vocabulary.

paragraphs.core_text: At that time the Living Spirit called one of his sons, one rich with power. He gave to him the leadership of the garments. Now, he himself [...] of [...] he hung them and set them up [...] of the Father of Life [...] he set up all things [...] he opened [...] ten firmaments [...] the wheel of the stars [...] them and the [...].
paragraphs.temporal_note: Highest substrate score in chapter (24.24). Pure cosmic construction narrative: Living Spirit delegates to his son, who constructs the cosmic architecture — firmaments, wheel of stars. 'Ten firmaments' and 'the wheel of the stars' are classic substrate cosmological vocabulary. Despite heavy lacunae, the structure describes emanation hierarchy and cosmic construction.

paragraphs.core_text: ⟨p.132⟩ The Living Spirit is like this: Just as [...] and an architect who might build a dwelling for the king, and divide it up into separate houses and [separate ...] everything that is required for beauty [...] and he cleans them. And also the stones [...] them for beauty and {loveliness}, and he arranges them and makes them so that should the king come and inhabit that palace, he might glorify him.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Architect-as-cosmic-builder analogy. While this maps cosmos→human craft rather than cosmos→cosmos, the demiurge-as-craftsman is one of the oldest cosmological figures in Near Eastern tradition. The analogy serves the cosmological teaching: it describes HOW the Living Spirit constructs the cosmic dwelling for the 'king' (the Ambassador). Low substrate vocabulary score (2.74) reflects analogical rather than technical cosmological language, but zero scores in all editorial categories. No marks of later editorial extension.

paragraphs.core_text: Furthermore, the Father of Life resembles a wise and skilled carpenter [...] before it was worked [...] before it was established and made beautiful and [...] carpenter [...] works in it, but [...] in him in his [...] in his understanding, and he brings the saw and the adze, and cuts it into separate pieces [...] it and he pulls the [...] it with the {plane} and he smooths it. He shall make many [...] wooden implements, arranging them shape by shape; he cuts and produces wooden implements from it, wooden implements of different kinds, (such as) dishes, bowls. This wood, that [...] since previously it had not been worked before it was sealed by [the ski]ll and wisdom of this dextrous carpenter. He cut it up into different sorts of implements useful to his master.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Seam flag fires for 'Furthermore' bridge connective, but OVERRIDDEN: content continues the same craft-analogy teaching sequence with no shift to institutional vocabulary. The carpenter metaphor parallels the architect metaphor in P3 — both describe how the cosmic builder shapes raw material (the mixture) into useful cosmic structures. The progression from architect (macro structure) to carpenter (working raw material into implements) mirrors the cosmic process: the universe is built, then the mixed substance is worked into functional cosmic apparatus. Zero scores in all editorial categories. The 'Furthermore' is intra-teaching progression, not editorial extension.

paragraphs.core_text: So is it also with the Father of Life. In his wisdom he has [...] in limbs [...] palace [...] in it or in a [...] useful [...] the ships of light [...] all the other works [...] in the [...] so that when the great king comes, he who is the Third Ambassador, who [...] he might dwell in this universe [...]
paragraphs.temporal_note: Application of the craft analogies back to cosmic entities: Father of Life, ships of light, Third Ambassador dwelling in the universe. 'So is it also with' closes the analogical sequence by mapping back to the cosmic system. This confirms P3-4 as pedagogical analogies within the cosmic teaching, not editorial extensions. 'Ships of light' is substrate cosmological vocabulary. The Third Ambassador as the 'great king' who inhabits the cosmic palace completes the architect/carpenter teaching.

paragraphs.core_text: ⟨p.133⟩ ... live. The light, however, that is in it [...] wise, and he takes it up to the land; but the waste and the Darkness will be gathered and thrown down to the abyss.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Cosmic eschatological summary: light ascends to the land of light, darkness/waste descends to the abyss. This is pure cosmic process teaching — the final separation. Despite zero substrate vocabulary score (the paragraph is very short at 35 words with heavy lacunae), the content is systematic cosmological process: the dual destiny of light and darkness. 'Gathered and thrown down to the abyss' describes cosmic-structural eschatology, not moral exhortation.
